chunks: O Allah! A drink from Thee with which our high lands get covered with green herbage, streams get flowing, our sides grow green, our fruits thrive, our cattle prosper, our far-flung areas get watered and our dry areas get its benefit
with Thy vast blessing and immeasurable grant on Thy distressed universe and Thy untamed beasts.

And pour upon us rain which is drenching, continuous and heavy; wherein one cycle of rain clashes with the other and one rain drop pushes another (into a continuous chain), its lightning should not be deceptive, its cheek not rainless, its white clouds not scattered and rain not light
so that the famine-stricken thrive with its abundant herbage and the drought stricken come to life with its bliss.
Certainly, Thou pourest down rain after the people lose hopes and spreadest Thy mercy, since Thou art the Guardian, the praiseworthy.

key_terms.الْمجْدِبُونَ: The famine-stricken or those suffering from drought
key_terms.الْمُسنِتُونَ: The drought-stricken or those affected by dry years
key_terms.سُقْيَا: A drink or provision, here referring to rain as sustenance
key_terms.نِجَاد: High lands or elevated areas of the earth

ai.seo_question: What is the Shia supplication for seeking rain from Allah?
ai.summary: Attributed to Imam Ali (AS) in *Nahj al-Balagha*, this supplication is traditionally recited during the *Salat al-Istisqa* (Prayer for Rain), reflecting the Shia practice of invoking divine mercy through eloquent, poetic Arabic. It emphasizes Allah’s power to send rain after people have lost hope, highlighting His mercy and guardianship.

en.sayed-ali-raza: O my Allāh! give rain from Thee with which our high lands get covered with green herbage, streams get flowing, our sides grow green, our fruits thrive, our cattle prosper, our far-flung areas get watered and our dry areas get its benefit,
with Thy vast blessing and immeasurable grant on Thy distressed universe and Thy untamed beasts.

And pour upon us rain which is drenching, continuous and heavy; wherein one cycle of rain clashes with the other and one rain drop pushes another (into a continuous chain), its lightning should not be deceptive, its cheek not rainless, its white clouds not scattered and rain not light,
so that the famine-stricken thrive with its abundant herbage and the drought stricken come to life with its bliss.
Certainly, Thou pourest down rain after the people lose hopes and spreadest Thy mercy, since Thou art the Guardian, the praiseworthy.
